claim: Upon cardiac pathological conditions such as ischemia, microenvironmental changes instruct a series of cellular responses that trigger cardiac fibroblasts-mediated tissue adaptation and inflammation.
source: Upon cardiac pathological conditions such as ischemia, microenvironmental changes instruct a series of cellular responses that trigger cardiac fibroblasts-mediated tissue adaptation and inflammation.
evidence: This is a general statement about cardiac pathology that draws from established scientific understanding of cardiac fibroblast responses to ischemia.

claim: Individual stimuli cause proliferative effects (PHH3+ mitotic cells, YAP translocation, PDGF secretion) or increase collagen presence.
source: Individual stimuli cause proliferative effects (PHH3+ mitotic cells, YAP translocation, PDGF secretion) or increase collagen presence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing measurements of PHH3+ cells, YAP localization, PDGF levels, and collagen staining under individual stimulus conditions.

claim: Only the combination of hypoxia and a simulated loss of contractility (2% strain) is able to additionally induce increased CF release of inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
source: Interestingly, only the combination of hypoxia and a simulated loss of contractility (2% strain) is able to additionally induce increased CF release of inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of cytokines (TGF-β, IL-1β) and MMPs in supernatants under combined stimulation conditions shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Within hours tissue necrosis and death of contractile cardiac myocytes occurs in the infarcted area giving rise to an inflammatory phase that recruits immune cells and activates quiescent cardiac fibroblasts.
source: within hours tissue necrosis and death of contractile cardiac myocytes occurs in the infarcted area giving rise to an inflammatory phase that recruits immune cells and activates quiescent cardiac fibroblasts (CFs); within a few days a proliferative phase begins, where activated CFs invade the infarcted area and contribute to degrading and replacing the extra-cellular matrix with a collagen-based scar; within weeks the maturation of the fibrotic scar is completed (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).

claim: Within a few days a proliferative phase begins, where activated CFs invade the infarcted area and contribute to degrading and replacing the extra-cellular matrix with a collagen-based scar.
source: within hours tissue necrosis and death of contractile cardiac myocytes occurs in the infarcted area giving rise to an inflammatory phase that recruits immune cells and activates quiescent cardiac fibroblasts (CFs); within a few days a proliferative phase begins, where activated CFs invade the infarcted area and contribute to degrading and replacing the extra-cellular matrix with a collagen-based scar; within weeks the maturation of the fibrotic scar is completed (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).

claim: Within weeks the maturation of the fibrotic scar is completed.
source: within hours tissue necrosis and death of contractile cardiac myocytes occurs in the infarcted area giving rise to an inflammatory phase that recruits immune cells and activates quiescent cardiac fibroblasts (CFs); within a few days a proliferative phase begins, where activated CFs invade the infarcted area and contribute to degrading and replacing the extra-cellular matrix with a collagen-based scar; within weeks the maturation of the fibrotic scar is completed (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Frangogiannis, 2014; Heusch et al., 2014).

claim: Excessive proliferation of CFs, phenotypic switch of CFs, high levels of inflammatory cytokines and humoral factors, unbalanced synthesis of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)-mediated degradation of ECM are generally regarded as hallmarks of early fibrotic tissue response.
source: Cellular and molecular events such as excessive proliferation of CFs, phenotypic switch of CFs, high levels of inflammatory cytokines and humoral factors, unbalanced synthesis of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)-mediated degradation of ECM are generally regarded as hallmarks of early fibrotic tissue response (Fan et al., 2012; Krenning et al., 2010; Porter and Turner, 2009; Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature (Fan et al., 2012; Krenning et al., 2010; Porter and Turner, 2009; Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014).

claim: The essential process of fibrotic tissue response often leads to excessive and adverse CFs remodeling of non-infarcted areas associated with cardiac dysfunction and increased mortality.
source: This essential process maintains tissue integrity, however, it often leads to excessive and adverse CFs remodeling of non-infarcted areas (Fan et al., 2012; Kania et al., 2009; Talman and Ruskoaho, 2016) associated with cardiac dysfunction and increased mortality (Okada et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Fan et al., 2012; Kania et al., 2009; Talman and Ruskoaho, 2016; Okada et al., 2005).

claim: The onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes mechanical strain to decrease (loss of contractility).
source: In general, the onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes alterations of specific environmental cues at the cellular scale: mechanical strain decreases (loss of contractility); oxygen and nutrient levels dramatically decrease (ischemia); levels of inflammatory cytokines increase (post-injury inflammatory response).
evidence: This is a general statement about pathological myocardial conditions based on established knowledge.

claim: The onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes oxygen and nutrient levels to dramatically decrease (ischemia).
source: In general, the onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes alterations of specific environmental cues at the cellular scale: mechanical strain decreases (loss of contractility); oxygen and nutrient levels dramatically decrease (ischemia); levels of inflammatory cytokines increase (post-injury inflammatory response).
evidence: This is a general statement about pathological myocardial conditions based on established knowledge.

claim: The onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes levels of inflammatory cytokines to increase (post-injury inflammatory response).
source: In general, the onset of pathological myocardial conditions causes alterations of specific environmental cues at the cellular scale: mechanical strain decreases (loss of contractility); oxygen and nutrient levels dramatically decrease (ischemia); levels of inflammatory cytokines increase (post-injury inflammatory response).
evidence: This is a general statement about pathological myocardial conditions based on established knowledge.

claim: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to increase ECM protein synthesis in CFs.
source: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to have the following effects on CFs: increased ECM protein synthesis (Carver et al., 1991); controversial proliferative behavior (Atance et al., 2004; Butt and Bishop, 1997; Dalla Costa et al., 2010; Liao et al., 2004), with recent reports of strain intensity-dependent effects (Ugolini et al., 2016); increased production of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cytokines such as TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta) (Leask, 2007) and TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) (Yokoyama et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Carver et al., 1991).

claim: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to cause controversial proliferative behavior in CFs, with recent reports of strain intensity-dependent effects.
source: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to have the following effects on CFs: increased ECM protein synthesis (Carver et al., 1991); controversial proliferative behavior (Atance et al., 2004; Butt and Bishop, 1997; Dalla Costa et al., 2010; Liao et al., 2004), with recent reports of strain intensity-dependent effects (Ugolini et al., 2016); increased production of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cytokines such as TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta) (Leask, 2007) and TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) (Yokoyama et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Atance et al., 2004; Butt and Bishop, 1997; Dalla Costa et al., 2010; Liao et al., 2004; Ugolini et al., 2016).

claim: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to increase production of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cytokines such as TGF-β and TNF-α in CFs.
source: The application of mechanical stress has been shown to have the following effects on CFs: increased ECM protein synthesis (Carver et al., 1991); controversial proliferative behavior (Atance et al., 2004; Butt and Bishop, 1997; Dalla Costa et al., 2010; Liao et al., 2004), with recent reports of strain intensity-dependent effects (Ugolini et al., 2016); increased production of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cytokines such as TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta) (Leask, 2007) and TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) (Yokoyama et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Leask, 2007; Yokoyama et al., 1999).

claim: CFs are sensitive to O2 level variations from physoxia (about 5–6% O2 in the myocardium).
source: While previous mechanical stress experiments were performed in a normoxic environment (NX, approximately 20% O2, the standard oxygen level of ambient air), CFs were shown to be sensitive to O2 level variations from physoxia (PX), defined as the physiologic oxygen level in living tissues (about 5–6% O2 in the myocardium [Gonschior et al., 1992; Roy et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2006; Winegrad et al., 1999]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Gonschior et al., 1992; Roy et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2006; Winegrad et al., 1999).

claim: Both hypoxia (1–3% O2) and normoxia induce a pro-inflammatory and fibrogenic phenotype in cultured CFs.
source: Both hypoxia (HX, 1–3% O2) and NX induce a pro-inflammatory and fibrogenic phenotype in cultured CFs (Roy et al., 2003; Sen and Roy, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Roy et al., 2003; Sen and Roy, 2010).

claim: Normoxic oxygen levels are perceived by CFs as a state of hyperoxia.
source: These findings imply that normoxic oxygen levels are perceived by CFs as a state of hyperoxia and that a significant bias exists when culturing CFs in non-physiological oxygen environments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings that both hypoxia and normoxia induce pro-inflammatory phenotypes in CFs.

claim: A significant bias exists when culturing CFs in non-physiological oxygen environments.
source: These findings imply that normoxic oxygen levels are perceived by CFs as a state of hyperoxia and that a significant bias exists when culturing CFs in non-physiological oxygen environments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings that both hypoxia and normoxia induce pro-inflammatory phenotypes in CFs.

claim: The exposure of CFs to hypoxia has been shown to induce collagen production and proliferation of CFs.
source: The exposure of CFs to HX has been shown to induce collagen production and proliferation of CFs (Gao et al., 2014; Tamamori et al., 1997), while studies suggest that MMP-based remodeling may not be triggered by HX alone (Riches et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Gao et al., 2014; Tamamori et al., 1997).

claim: Studies suggest that MMP-based remodeling may not be triggered by hypoxia alone.
source: The exposure of CFs to HX has been shown to induce collagen production and proliferation of CFs (Gao et al., 2014; Tamamori et al., 1997), while studies suggest that MMP-based remodeling may not be triggered by HX alone (Riches et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Riches et al., 2009).

claim: There is no report of cardiac cells subjected to simultaneous mechanical strain and controlled oxygen changes.
source: To date, no comprehensive model is able to recapitulate early cellular events taking place after acute myocardial injury and there is no report of cardiac cells subjected to simultaneous mechanical strain and controlled oxygen changes, two major environmental variables involved in cardiac injury and CF adaptive responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Shortly after an ischemic myocardial insult, tissue oxygen levels drop from approximately 5–6% O2 to near-zero.
source: Shortly after an ischemic myocardial insult (e.g., acute coronary artery occlusion) tissue oxygen levels drop from approximately 5–6% O2 (Gonschior et al., 1992; Sen et al., 2006; Winegrad et al., 1999) to near-zero (Roy et al., 2003), rapidly inducing loss of cardiac myocytes contractility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Gonschior et al., 1992; Sen et al., 2006; Winegrad et al., 1999; Roy et al., 2003).

claim: Ischemic myocardial insult rapidly induces loss of cardiac myocytes contractility.
source: Shortly after an ischemic myocardial insult (e.g., acute coronary artery occlusion) tissue oxygen levels drop from approximately 5–6% O2 (Gonschior et al., 1992; Sen et al., 2006; Winegrad et al., 1999) to near-zero (Roy et al., 2003), rapidly inducing loss of cardiac myocytes contractility.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of cardiac physiology.

claim: Tissue bulging and dilations are commonly observed together with loss of contractile function in injured myocardial tissue.
source: Dramatic alterations of injured myocardial tissue also take place in early timeframes: tissue bulging and dilations are commonly observed together with loss of contractile function (Eek et al., 2010; Pfeffer and Braunwald, 1990; Picard et al., 1990; Tennant and Wiggers, 1935).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Eek et al., 2010; Pfeffer and Braunwald, 1990; Picard et al., 1990; Tennant and Wiggers, 1935).

claim: Cardiac imaging studies agree that global strains are abruptly reduced shortly after myocardial insult.
source: Cardiac imaging studies agree in the interpretation that global strains are abruptly reduced shortly after myocardial insult (Flachskampf et al., 2011; Hoit, 2011; Mollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Flachskampf et al., 2011; Hoit, 2011; Mollema et al., 2010).

claim: Strains in ischemic/injured regions have been reported to be 2–4 fold lower than in healthy myocardial regions (e.g. less than 3% in ischemic regions versus approximately 10% in healthy regions).
source: Quantitatively, strain values recorded vary significantly throughout the heart. Although absolute values may depend on imaging algorithms, strains in ischemic/injured regions have been reported to be 2–4 fold lower than in healthy myocardial regions (e.g. less than 3% in ischemic regions versus approximately 10% in healthy regions [Dandel et al., 2009; Vartdal et al., 2007]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Dandel et al., 2009; Vartdal et al., 2007).

claim: Environmental changes and the following initial cellular responses happen in a timeframe of hours, as shown in vitro and in vivo.
source: These environmental changes and the following initial cellular responses happen in a timeframe of hours, as shown in vitro (van Nieuwenhoven et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2007, 2009) as well as in vivo (Guillén et al., 1995; Morishita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (van Nieuwenhoven et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2007, 2009; Guillén et al., 1995; Morishita et al., 2015).

claim: An intense staining for collagen I localized to perinuclear regions of CFs was observed after 24 hr under specific stimulations.
source: While CFs normally exhibit diffuse cytoplasmic staining for collagen I, an intense staining localized to perinuclear regions of CFs was observed after 24 hr under specific stimulations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in collagen I was similarly triggered by hypoxia alone and 8% strain alone.
source: Based on analysis of intracellular fluorescence intensity, we found that the increase in collagen I was similarly triggered by HX alone and 8% strain alone (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity analyses shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No significant synergy was found for hypoxia and mechanical strain on collagen I levels: levels of collagen I are similarly elevated in all hypoxia conditions regardless of strain applied.
source: No significant synergy was found for the two stimulations: levels of collagen I are similarly elevated in all HX conditions regardless of strain applied.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the collagen I fluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Collagen I staining exhibits similar intensity in all 8% strain conditions regardless of the oxygen stimulation employed.
source: Correspondingly, collagen I staining exhibits similar intensity in all 8% strain conditions regardless of the oxygen stimulation employed.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the collagen I fluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After only 12 hr of stimulation, collagen I fluorescence showed similar trends, with the exception of hypoxia combined with 8% cyclic strain which provided a greater synergistic effect compared to the single stimulations.
source: After only 12 hr of stimulation, collagen I fluorescence showed similar trends, with the exception of HX combined with 8% cyclic strain which provided a greater synergistic effect compared to the single stimulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Culturing CFs at normoxia levels does not induce significant changes in collagen I presence.
source: We also report that culturing CFs at NX levels does not induce significant changes in collagen I presence.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the collagen I fluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The expression of MMP-2 and MMP-3 in CFs supernatants was significantly influenced by combined mechanical strain and oxygen changes.
source: The expression of MMP-2 and MMP-3 in CFs supernatants (Figure 1CD) was significantly influenced by combined mechanical strain and oxygen changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: MMP-2 was more prominently expressed than MMP-3 (>100X higher).
source: MMP-2 was more prominently expressed than MMP-3 (>100X higher).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the measured protein levels shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: A significant two-fold increase in MMP-2 and MMP-3 expression was induced by the combination of hypoxia and mechanical strain, with a more pronounced increase observed in the hypoxia/2% strain combined conditions.
source: Nevertheless, the expression of both enzymes was similarly regulated by the pattern of stimulations applied: a significant two-fold increase in MMP-2 and MMP-3 expression was induced by the combination of HX and mechanical strain, with a more pronounced increase observed in the HX/2% strain combined conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: MMP-3 expression was negatively affected when CFs were subjected to mechanical strain at physoxia or hypoxia stimulus alone.
source: MMP-3 expression was negatively affected when CFs were subjected to mechanical strain at PX or HX stimulus alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Without application of cyclic strain, a two-fold significant increase in the number of mitotic cells was observed when CFs were stimulated with hypoxia compared to their physoxia counterparts.
source: Without application of cyclic strain, we observed a two-fold significant increase in the number of mitotic cells (Figure 2B) when CFs were stimulated with HX compared to their PX counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of mitotic cell fraction shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mechanical strain significantly impacted cell proliferation within the physoxia culture condition: culturing CFs at physoxia and subjecting them to 2% strain induced a striking increase in mitotic cells compared to no strain control and 8% strain cultures.
source: Mechanical strain significantly impacted cell proliferation within the PX culture condition: culturing CFs at PX and subjecting them to 2% strain induced a striking increase in mitotic cells compared to no strain control and 8% strain cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of mitotic cell fraction shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The strain intensity-dependent effect on CF proliferation is in line with previous investigations of CF proliferation under mechanical strain in normoxia conditions.
source: This strain intensity-dependent effect is in line with our previous investigations of CF proliferation under mechanical strain in NX conditions (Ugolini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ugolini et al., 2016).

claim: After 12 hr of stimulation, the proliferative increase with hypoxia is not statistically significant.
source: After 12 hr of stimulation, the proliferative increase with HX is not statistically significant, while we report a significant synergistic decrease of mitotic cells induced by the combination of 8% strain and HX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 12 hr of stimulation, a significant synergistic decrease of mitotic cells was induced by the combination of 8% strain and hypoxia.
source: After 12 hr of stimulation, the proliferative increase with HX is not statistically significant, while we report a significant synergistic decrease of mitotic cells induced by the combination of 8% strain and HX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CFs exhibited much greater mitosis under normoxia environments (approx. 5% mitotic cells) compared to physoxia environments (approx. 1% mitotic cells) denoting a strong proliferative effect of standard cell culture environments.
source: Interestingly, CFs exhibited much greater mitosis under NX environments (approx. 5% mitotic cells) compared to PX environments (approx. 1% mitotic cells) denoting a strong proliferative effect of standard cell culture environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of mitotic cell fraction shown in Figure 2B.

claim: YAP is a transcription factor mainly known as the principal effector of the Hippo proliferative pathway, a crucial pathway involved in cardiac regeneration and repair.
source: Further, we evaluated the effects of the environmental changes on YAP, a transcription factor mainly known as the principal effector of the Hippo proliferative pathway, a crucial pathway involved in cardiac regeneration and repair (Papizan and Olson, 2014; Xin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Papizan and Olson, 2014; Xin et al., 2013).

claim: Recent literature has described a parallel mechano-sensing associated role of YAP.
source: Recent literature has also described a parallel mechano-sensing associated role of YAP (Dupont et al., 2011; Mosqueira et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Dupont et al., 2011; Mosqueira et al., 2014).

claim: YAP translocation from cytoplasm to nucleus leads to inactivation of Hippo pathway and a subsequent increase in cell proliferation.
source: YAP translocation from cytoplasm to nucleus leads to inactivation of Hippo pathway and a subsequent increase in cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of the Hippo pathway.

claim: The fraction of CFs displaying nuclear YAP is influenced by the combination of stimuli with trends similar to the fraction of mitotic cells.
source: We therefore quantified nuclear localization of YAP by means of immunofluorescence, which revealed that the fraction of CFs displaying nuclear YAP is influenced by the combination of stimuli with trends similar to the fraction of mitotic cells (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of nuclear YAP shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In CFs cultured at physoxia, 2% strain induces higher YAP translocation into cell nuclei.
source: In CFs cultured at PX, 2% strain induces higher YAP translocation into cell nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of nuclear YAP shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CFs solely exposed to hypoxia environment show a significant two-fold increase in nuclear YAP compared to a physoxia environment.
source: CFs solely exposed to HX environment show a significant two-fold increase in nuclear YAP compared to a PX environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of nuclear YAP shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mechanical strain shows a negative interaction when combined with hypoxia, with CFs subject to hypoxia/8% strain condition showing lower fractions of nuclear YAP compared to CFs subject to hypoxia alone.
source: Mechanical strain shows a negative interaction when combined with HX, with CFs subject to HX/8% strain condition showing lower fractions of nuclear YAP compared to CFs subject to HX alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of nuclear YAP shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CFs cultured in a normoxia environment show a three-fold increase in nuclear YAP compared to physoxia conditions.
source: Interestingly, CFs cultured in an NX environment show a three-fold increase in nuclear YAP compared to PX conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analyses of nuclear YAP shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PDGF has been described as a potent mitogen for CFs.
source: PDGF has been described as a potent mitogen for CFs, is significantly over-expressed in in vivo models of heart injury (Zhao et al., 2011), and has recently been studied as a putative pharmacological target for attenuating adverse effects of cardiac fibrotic disease (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: PDGF is significantly over-expressed in in vivo models of heart injury.
source: PDGF has been described as a potent mitogen for CFs, is significantly over-expressed in in vivo models of heart injury (Zhao et al., 2011), and has recently been studied as a putative pharmacological target for attenuating adverse effects of cardiac fibrotic disease (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: PDGF has recently been studied as a putative pharmacological target for attenuating adverse effects of cardiac fibrotic disease.
source: PDGF has been described as a potent mitogen for CFs, is significantly over-expressed in in vivo models of heart injury (Zhao et al., 2011), and has recently been studied as a putative pharmacological target for attenuating adverse effects of cardiac fibrotic disease (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Liu et al., 2014).

claim: A four-fold increase in the detected amounts of PDGF was observed in hypoxia compared to physoxia, without application of cyclic strain.
source: Expression of PDGF in CF culture supernatant (Figure 2E) was significantly affected by HX stimulation: a four-fold increase in the detected amounts of PDGF was observed in HX compared to PX, without application of cyclic strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mechanical stimulation showed a negative interaction with the hypoxia-induced secretion of PDGF: while levels of PDGF expression remain elevated under hypoxia/2% strain, application of 8% cyclic strain shows a negative regulation of PDGF secretion back to physoxia levels of expression.
source: Mechanical stimulation showed a negative interaction with the HX-induced secretion of PDGF: while levels of PDGF expression remain elevated under HX/2% strain, application of 8% cyclic strain shows a negative regulation of PDGF secretion back to PX levels of expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Recent reports suggest that CFs play a key role in modulating a functional inflammasome that includes inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines.
source: The precise contribution of CFs in the regulation of the early inflammatory response in myocardial remodeling is still to be determined, however, recent reports suggest that CFs play a key role in modulating a functional inflammasome that includes inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines (Kawaguchi et al., 2011; Lindner et al., 2014; Turner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kawaguchi et al., 2011; Lindner et al., 2014; Turner, 2016).

claim: CFs stimulated with a combination of hypoxia and mechanical strain (specifically 2% strain) were found to increase secretion of TGF-β by approximately two-fold.
source: CFs stimulated with a combination of HX and mechanical strain (specifically 2% strain) were found to increase secretion of TGF-β by approximately two-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CFs cultured at physoxia expressed lower amounts of TGF-β, regardless of the mechanical strain applied.
source: CFs cultured at PX expressed lower amounts of TGF-β, regardless of the mechanical strain applied (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TGF-β is a major contributor to fibrotic responses, widely studied across a variety of tissues and organs.
source: TGF-β is a major contributor to fibrotic responses, widely studied across a variety of tissues and organs.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of TGF-β.

claim: During post-injury myocardial remodeling, TGF-β is known to stimulate a wide range of CF responses from phenotypic switch to collagen synthesis and ECM remodeling.
source: During post-injury myocardial remodeling, TGF-β is known to stimulate a wide range of CF responses from phenotypic switch to collagen synthesis and ECM remodeling (Leask, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Leask, 2007).

claim: IL1-β is one of the first cytokines detected in vivo after myocardial injury.
source: IL1-β is one of the first cytokines detected in vivo after myocardial injury (Guillén et al., 1995) and is known to stimulate CF response including the production of MMPs (Brown et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2008; Siwik et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Guillén et al., 1995).

claim: IL1-β is known to stimulate CF response including the production of MMPs.
source: IL1-β is one of the first cytokines detected in vivo after myocardial injury (Guillén et al., 1995) and is known to stimulate CF response including the production of MMPs (Brown et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2008; Siwik et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Brown et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2008; Siwik et al., 2000).

claim: A significant two-fold increase in IL1-β expression occurred only when CFs were subjected to the combination of hypoxia and mechanical strain, particularly with 2% strain.
source: Interestingly, we found that a significant two-fold increase in IL1-β expression occurred only when CFs were subjected to the combination of HX and mechanical strain, particularly with 2% strain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Extremely low amounts of TNF-α were detected, with non-significant variations across all stimulation conditions.
source: Conversely, we observed how the expression of inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 was not influenced by the application of environmental stimuli. We detected extremely low amounts of TNF-α (Figure 3C), with non-significant variations across all stimulation conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IL-6 was abundantly expressed by CFs yet none of the differences in its expression were found to be statistically significant.
source: IL-6 (Figure 3D) was abundantly expressed by CFs yet none of the differences in its expression were found to be statistically significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The hallmark of myofibroblast phenotype switch is the expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) that, by being incorporated into actin stress fibers, confers increased mechanical and motile capabilities to differentiated myofibroblasts.
source: The hallmark of this phenotype switch is the expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) that, by being incorporated into actin stress fibers, confers increased mechanical and motile capabilities to differentiated myofibroblasts (Baum and Duffy, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Baum and Duffy, 2011).

claim: A basal expression of cytoplasmic αSMA is present in all combined stimulation conditions.
source: Immunostainings of CFs (Figure 4) reveal that a basal expression of cytoplasmic αSMA is present in all combined stimulation conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4.

claim: Under no experimental condition did CFs exhibit co-localization of αSMA and actin stress fibers, indicating that differentiation into myofibroblasts was not induced by the pattern of environmental stimuli.
source: However, under no experimental condition did CFs exhibit co-localization of αSMA (red) and actin stress fibers (green), indicating that differentiation into myofibroblasts was not induced by our pattern of environmental stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stimulating CFs by supplementing TGF-β in the culture medium caused the appearance of cells exhibiting superimposed αSMA and actin signal (yellow).
source: Conversely, stimulating CFs by supplementing TGF-β in the culture medium (a known inducer of CF differentiation to myofibroblasts) caused the appearance of cells exhibiting superimposed αSMA and actin signal (yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increase in cell proliferation is mediated by the Hippo pathway given the correlation between nuclear YAP translocation and mitotic cells (PHH3+).
source: We propose that the increase in cell proliferation is mediated by the Hippo pathway given the correlation between nuclear YAP translocation and mitotic cells (PHH3+).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation observed between YAP localization and mitotic cell counts.

claim: In contrast with other studies performed at normoxia, YAP nuclear translocation is not related to increasing cyclic mechanical strain.
source: We found, however, that in contrast with other studies performed at NX (Codelia et al., 2014), YAP nuclear translocation is not related to increasing cyclic mechanical strain.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current study's findings with previous literature (Codelia et al., 2014).

claim: An increased secretion of mitogenic PDGF by CFs at hypoxia suggests a possible autocrine CF mechanism aimed at modulating proliferation upon pathological myocardial conditions.
source: In addition, an increased secretion of mitogenic PDGF by CFs at HX suggests a possible autocrine CF mechanism aimed at modulating proliferation upon pathological myocardial conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the PDGF expression data.

claim: Hypoxia alone causes an increased collagen presence in CFs cultures, which is consistent with data obtained in previous works focused on collagen production by CFs subject to hypoxia.
source: We also showed that hypoxia alone causes an increased collagen presence in CFs cultures. This is consistent with data obtained in previous works focused on collagen production by CFs subject to HX (Tamamori et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citation to previous literature (Tamamori et al., 1997).

claim: Hypoxia alone induces pro-fibrotic responses in CFs.
source: We therefore demonstrated how HX alone induces pro-fibrotic responses in CFs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collagen I data.

claim: The combination of hypoxia and mechanical strain incrementally instructed further pathological cell responses.
source: A significant novel insight observed in the present study is that the combination of HX and mechanical strain incrementally instructed further pathological cell responses.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: The production of pro-fibrotic TGF-β, inflammatory cytokine IL1-β and matrix-degrading enzymes (MMP-2 and MMP-3) significantly increased only when cells were subject to combined hypoxia and low levels of cyclic strain (hypoxia/2% strain).
source: Indeed, the production of pro-fibrotic TGF-β, inflammatory cytokine IL1-β and matrix-degrading enzymes (MMP-2 and MMP-3) significantly increased only when cells were subject to combined HX and low levels of cyclic strain (HX/2% strain).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Previous studies reported inhibitory effects of hypoxia alone on MMP expression.
source: MMPs are known to be primarily involved in the remodeling of the injured myocardium and it is worth noting that previous studies reported inhibitory effects of HX alone on MMP expression (Riches et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Riches et al., 2009).

claim: In another study, mechanical stress did not alter MMP expression unless cells were cultured in serum deprivation.
source: In another study, mechanical stress did not alter MMP expression unless cells were cultured in serum deprivation (Tyagi et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Tyagi et al., 1998).

claim: Literature suggests a direct effect of TGF-β and IL1-β on the expression of MMPs in CFs.
source: In addition, literature suggests a direct effect of TGF-β and IL1-β on the expression of MMPs in CFs (Brown et al., 2007; Stawowy et al., 2004) and we observed how the expression levels of TGF-β and IL1-β under combined stimulation are in line with the altered expression of MMPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Brown et al., 2007; Stawowy et al., 2004).

claim: The expression levels of TGF-β and IL1-β under combined stimulation are in line with the altered expression of MMPs.
source: In addition, literature suggests a direct effect of TGF-β and IL1-β on the expression of MMPs in CFs (Brown et al., 2007; Stawowy et al., 2004) and we observed how the expression levels of TGF-β and IL1-β under combined stimulation are in line with the altered expression of MMPs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the expression patterns of TGF-β, IL1-β, and MMPs.

claim: No experimental condition led to myofibroblast differentiation, with the exception of the positive control (additional biochemical stimulation with TGF-β), thus highlighting the importance of soluble pro-fibrotic factors for this aspect of CF pathological activation.
source: Notably, no experimental condition led to myofibroblast differentiation, with the exception of the positive control (additional biochemical stimulation with TGF-β), thus highlighting the importance of soluble pro-fibrotic factors for this aspect of CF pathological activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the αSMA staining results shown in Figure 4.

claim: When cells were subject to physiological cyclic strain (8% strain) together with hypoxia condition, most of the pathological CF responses were not observed and only a modest increase in collagen presence was found.
source: Intriguingly, we found that when cells were subject to physiological cyclic strain (8% strain) together with HX condition, most of the above pathological CF responses were not observed and we found only a modest increase in collagen presence.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across multiple assays.

claim: When oxygen conditions resemble those of healthy tissue (physoxia), cyclic mechanical strain only results in increased collagen presence (at 8% strain) or in increased proliferation (at 2% strain).
source: Similarly, when oxygen conditions resemble those of healthy tissue (PX), cyclic mechanical strain only results in increased collagen presence (at 8% strain) or in increased proliferation (at 2% strain).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across multiple assays.

claim: These results are in line with previous studies (performed in normoxia environments) on mechanically stimulated CFs.
source: These results are in line with previous studies (performed in NX environments) on mechanically stimulated CFs (Carver et al., 1991; Husse et al., 2007; Ugolini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Carver et al., 1991; Husse et al., 2007; Ugolini et al., 2016).

claim: CFs respond differently to different regimes of cyclic strain, to different oxygen conditions and to combinations of these.
source: Overall, these outcomes suggest that CFs respond differently to different regimes of cyclic strain, to different oxygen conditions and to combinations of these.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall experimental results.

claim: In the context of an acute myocardial insult, loss of contractility and decrease in sensed oxygen levels are able to instruct a consistent response of CFs that involves matrix remodeling, inflammatory and proliferative behaviors.
source: In the context of an acute myocardial insult, loss of contractility and decrease in sensed oxygen levels are able to instruct a consistent response of CFs that involves matrix remodeling, inflammatory and proliferative behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall experimental results.

claim: A mechanical environment resembling full contractility (8% strain) may hold a protective potential and resulted in attenuating CFs inflammatory, remodeling and pro-fibrotic responses taking place in hypoxia.
source: Our combined conditions allowed us to report that a mechanical environment resembling full contractility (8% strain) may hold a protective potential and resulted in attenuating CFs inflammatory, remodeling and pro-fibrotic responses taking place in HX.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The on-chip model correlates well with quantitative readouts involving ECM, ECM-remodeling enzymes (collagen and MMPs expression) and proliferative effects from standard in vitro models.
source: Our model correlates well with quantitative readouts involving ECM, ECM-remodeling enzymes (collagen and MMPs expression) and proliferative effects, although contradictory studies also showed decreased CF proliferation under pro-fibrotic stimuli.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current study's results with literature data shown in Table 2.

claim: MMP levels in serum were shown to increase by approximately two-fold in patients after 24 hr from acute myocardial injury diagnosis.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Morishita et al., 2015).

evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison with literature and the current study's results.
